section.title: The Yoke of Babylon and Hananiah
section.sectionRationale: Jeremiah wears an actual wooden yoke to dramatize submission to Babylon as God's appointed discipline, sending the same message to surrounding kings and to Zedekiah himself. The confrontation comes to a head when the prophet Hananiah publicly breaks that yoke and promises deliverance within two years, forcing the sharpest test yet of how a true word from God can be told from a comforting lie.
section.thesis: God has placed the whole region under Babylon's yoke for a set time, and any prophet, like Hananiah, who promises quick deliverance instead is prophesying a lie, so that breaking a wooden yoke only earns the nation an iron one, and death for the false prophet who broke it.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the yoke of Babylon proclaimed to Judah and the surrounding nations, a warning about the temple vessels and false hopes of their quick return, Hananiah breaking Jeremiah's yoke before the people, and Jeremiah's grim reply of an iron yoke and Hananiah's death within the year.

verses.text: At the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah son of Josiah king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD.

This is what the LORD said to me: 
“Make for yourself a {{ol|yoke}} out of leather straps and put it on your neck.
Send word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon through the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.
Give them a message from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, to relay to their masters:
By My great power and outstretched arm, I made the earth and the men and beasts on the face of it, and I give it to whom I please.
So now I have placed all these lands under the authority of My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. I have even made the beasts of the field subject to him.
All nations will serve him and his son and grandson, until the time of his own land comes; then many nations and great kings will enslave him.

As for the nation or kingdom that does not serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and does not place its neck under his yoke, I will punish that nation by sword and famine and plague, declares the LORD, until I have destroyed it by his hand.
But as for you, do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your interpreters of dreams, your mediums, or your sorcerers who declare, ‘You will not serve the king of Babylon.’
For they prophesy to you a {{sheqer|lie}} that will serve to remove you from your land; I will banish you and you will perish.
But the nation that will put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave in its own land, to cultivate it and reside in it, declares the LORD.”
And to Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke the same message: “Put your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon; serve him and his people, and live!
Why should you and your people die by sword and famine and plague, as the LORD has decreed against any nation that does not serve the king of Babylon?
Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say, ‘You must not serve the king of Babylon,’ for they are prophesying to you a lie.
For I have not sent them, declares the LORD, and yet they are prophesying falsely in My name; therefore I will banish you, and you will perish, you and the prophets who prophesy to you.”

units.label: The temple vessels and false hopes
units.note: not soon, but at God's appointed time

verses.text: Then I said to the priests and to all this people, “This is what the LORD says: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying, ‘Look, very soon now the articles from the house of the LORD will be brought back from Babylon.’ They are prophesying to you a lie.
Do not listen to them. Serve the king of Babylon and live! Why should this city become a ruin?

If they are indeed prophets and the word of the LORD is with them, let them now plead with the LORD of Hosts that the articles remaining in the house of the LORD, in the palace of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem, not be taken to Babylon.
For this is what the LORD of Hosts says about the pillars, the sea, the bases, and the rest of the articles that remain in this city,
which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take when he carried Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon, along with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem.
Yes, this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says about the articles that remain in the house of the LORD, in the palace of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem:
‘They will be carried to Babylon and will remain there until the day I attend to them again,’ declares the LORD. ‘Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place.’”

units.label: Hananiah breaks the yoke
units.note: a wooden yoke shattered in the LORD's house

verses.text: In the fifth month of that same year, the fourth year, near the beginning of the reign of King Zedekiah of Judah, the prophet Hananiah son of Azzur, who was from Gibeon, said to me in the house of the LORD in the presence of the priests and all the people:
“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.
Within two years I will restore to this place all the articles of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon removed from here and carried to Babylon.

And I will restore to this place Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, along with all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon,’ declares the LORD, ‘for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.’”
Then the prophet Jeremiah replied to the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD.
“Amen!” Jeremiah said. “May the LORD do so! May the LORD fulfill the words you have prophesied, and may He restore the articles of His house and all the exiles back to this place from Babylon.
Nevertheless, listen now to this message I am speaking in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people.
The prophets of old who preceded you and me prophesied war, disaster, and plague against many lands and great kingdoms.
As for the prophet who prophesies peace, only if the word of the prophet comes true will the prophet be recognized as one the LORD has truly sent.”
Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it.

And in the presence of all the people Hananiah proclaimed, “This is what the LORD says: ‘In this way, within two years I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon off the neck of all the nations.’” 
At this, Jeremiah the prophet went on his way.

units.label: An iron yoke, and Hananiah's death
units.note: the truth of a prophet's word tested

verses.text: But shortly after Hananiah the prophet had broken the yoke off his neck, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
“Go and tell Hananiah that this is what the LORD says: ‘You have broken a yoke of wood, but in its place you have fashioned a yoke of iron.’

For this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations to make them serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they will serve him. I have even given him control of the beasts of the field.’”
Then the prophet Jeremiah said to the prophet Hananiah, “Listen, Hananiah! The LORD did not send you, but you have persuaded this people to trust in a lie.
Therefore this is what the LORD says: ‘I am about to remove you from the face of the earth. You will die this year because you have preached rebellion against the LORD.’”
And in the seventh month of that very year, the prophet Hananiah died.

ol.gloss: A yoke, the wooden crossbar laid on an animal's neck for labor or submission, worn literally by Jeremiah as a sign that Judah and the surrounding nations must submit to Babylon's rule as God's appointed discipline. Hananiah's breaking of this yoke was meant to picture liberation, but God turns it into a prophecy of even harsher bondage, a wooden yoke replaced by one of iron.

sheqer.gloss: A lie or falsehood, the word Jeremiah repeatedly uses for the message of the prophets promising quick deliverance from Babylon. The same word closes the Hananiah episode, 'you have persuaded this people to trust in a sheqer', showing that comforting words not actually sent by God are, however sincerely delivered, still a lie.

basic.context: Jeremiah wears an actual wooden yoke around his neck as a sign that Judah, along with the surrounding nations of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, must submit to Babylon's rule, since God has appointed Nebuchadnezzar as His servant for this season. When the prophet Hananiah publicly breaks that yoke and promises the exiles and temple vessels will return within two years, Jeremiah's initial hope, 'Amen, may the LORD do so,' gives way to a stark verdict: Hananiah's message was never from God, and he will die within the year for persuading the people to trust a lie.
basic.hermeneutics: This narrative gives a real, concrete test for discerning true from false prophecy, stated directly in 28:9, a peace-prophecy is proven true only when it actually comes to pass. The uncomfortable truth the passage refuses to soften is that a sincere, popular, hopeful message, delivered confidently in God's name and even by another recognized prophet, can still be entirely false, and following it leads only to greater bondage.
basic.originalLanguages: The ol, yoke, Jeremiah wears is a vivid, physical sign of submission, and its breaking by Hananiah is meant to dramatize liberation, but God turns the image against him, a wooden yoke replaced by iron, harsher bondage rather than freedom. Throughout, the message of the peace-prophets is repeatedly called sheqer, a lie, regardless of how sincerely or popularly it was delivered, showing that good intentions or popularity do not make a message true.
basic.typology: The yoke of submission to a foreign power that God calls His people to bear anticipates the New Testament's call to submit even to difficult, imposed authorities as part of God's sovereign ordering of history, Romans 13:1. Hananiah's confident but false prophecy anticipates the New Testament's repeated warnings about false teachers who speak comforting words that are never actually from God.
basic.christ: Christ invites His followers to take His yoke instead, Matthew 11:29-30, a yoke that, unlike Babylon's, is easy and light, the ultimate contrast to every burdensome and false yoke offered by human power or human deception. Where Hananiah offered a false, premature liberation that led only to harsher bondage, Christ offers a true and lasting rest that comes only through genuine submission to Him, the pattern this whole episode of false hope versus true submission anticipates.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over pagan empires, explicitly calling Nebuchadnezzar 'My servant' and giving him authority over nations by His own appointment, not merely allowing it. Yet God is also a God of truth who will not let a false message stand indefinitely, however sincerely or popularly proclaimed, holding false prophets accountable and vindicating His true word within the timeframe He sets.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 11:29-30 contrasts every burdensome yoke with Christ's own yoke, which is easy and light. Romans 13:1-2 teaches submission to governing authorities as part of God's sovereign ordering, echoing the call to bear Babylon's yoke as God's appointed discipline. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 gives the same test cited in Jeremiah 28:9, a prophet's word is proven true only by its fulfillment. 2 Peter 2:1-3 warns of false teachers exploiting people with fabricated messages, exactly Hananiah's pattern.
basic.oneStory: The yoke of Babylon, worn literally by Jeremiah and broken falsely by Hananiah, shows how tempting it is to trade God's hard but true word for a comforting lie, and how much heavier the bondage becomes when that lie is believed. That whole pattern of false, burdensome yokes finds its answer in Christ, who offers His people a yoke that is genuinely easy and a burden that is genuinely light, the true liberation Hananiah only pretended to offer.

context.literary:
Chapters 27 and 28 are one unit, and the editors have bound them with a shared vocabulary: yoke, serve, lie, break, and the repeated phrase 'in the presence of all the people.' The movement is a double address followed by a duel. In 27:1 to 11 Jeremiah speaks to the foreign envoys, in 27:12 to 15 to the king, and in 27:16 to 22 to the priests and people, with the same message each time and a widening of the false hope it targets, from rebellion, to Zedekiah's own prophets, to the temple vessels. Chapter 28 then turns the theory into a confrontation. Hananiah speaks first, Jeremiah answers, Hananiah acts, and Jeremiah, silent for a time, is given a word.

The narrator shifts into the first person at 27:2 ('This is what the LORD said to me') and stays there, so the reader hears Jeremiah's own memory of the encounter. Notice the structure of the drama in chapter 28. Hananiah's oracle in verses 2 to 4 is formally flawless: the messenger formula, the divine title, a specific date, and a specific promise. Jeremiah's reply is a model of restraint. He says 'Amen,' states the test, and goes on his way, verse 11. The text lets the false prophet have his moment before the true word arrives.

There is also a play on wood and iron. A wooden yoke is replaced by an iron one in 28:13, which makes the breaking itself the cause of the harsher bondage. The chapter ends with a death notice that is almost clinical: 'in the seventh month of that very year, the prophet Hananiah died,' 28:17. The dates in 28:1 and 28:17 frame a two-month interval in which the issue was decided, a pointed contrast with Hananiah's 'within two years.'
context.historical:
The setting is about 594 to 593 BC, the fourth year of Zedekiah. Nebuchadnezzar had taken Jeconiah, the royal family and the craftsmen to Babylon in 597, and with them much of the temple's treasure, 2 Kings 24:12 to 14. Zedekiah, installed as a puppet, ruled a shaken and divided city. The envoys of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, 27:3, had come to Jerusalem, and the likeliest reason is a plan for a joint revolt against Babylon. Every kingdom on the list was in the Babylonian sphere and had reason to hope for a change. In that atmosphere the prophets promising a swift reversal were the voice of popular opinion. Jeremiah 51:59 notes that Zedekiah himself, or his envoy, travelled to Babylon in this same fourth year, which may show that the king was uncertain.

The yoke was a familiar object: a wooden crossbar with leather straps and a pole, put on oxen and used in the ancient world as a symbol of subjection to a conqueror. Jeremiah's use of it belongs to the prophets' practice of enacted parables. Isaiah had walked about naked and barefoot as a sign against Egypt and Cush, Isaiah 20:2.

Hananiah was from Gibeon, a priestly town, Joshua 21:17, and he spoke in the temple 'in the presence of the priests and all the people,' 28:1. His oracle echoed an older and respectable tradition, the confidence in Zion's inviolability that Isaiah's generation had found vindicated in 701. He may well have believed what he said. The text also notes that 'the prophets of old' had mostly prophesied war, 28:8, which tells us the standard of the true prophet's task: to confront a settled nation with a word that overturns its comfort.
context.canonical:
The yoke is one of the Bible's great controlling images, and these chapters hold a hinge in its development. It begins as a sign of covenant blessing: 'I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness,' Leviticus 26:13. It becomes a curse for covenant breaking, since Deuteronomy 28:48 warns of an iron yoke on the neck, and Hananiah's iron yoke in Jeremiah 28:13 is the fulfilment of that warning. Jeremiah's ministry thus applies the covenant curses of Deuteronomy to his generation. The promise of broken bonds is not abandoned. It is postponed to the Book of Consolation, 'I will break the yoke off their necks,' Jeremiah 30:8, and the next two chapters set that promise beside a call to patience.

The discernment of prophecy runs through the whole Torah. Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5 deals with the prophet whose sign comes true but who leads people to other gods, and Deuteronomy 18:20 to 22 with the prophet whose word does not come true. Jeremiah 28:9 stands on the second text, and the same book gives the tests of faithfulness to God's earlier word in 23:9 to 40. The surprising theme that the LORD can use pagan power as His servant, 27:6, is set beside Isaiah's Cyrus, Isaiah 45:1, and Daniel's lesson that God 'gives it to whom He wishes,' Daniel 4:17.

In the New Testament the yoke is re-voiced by Jesus, Matthew 11:29 to 30, and Paul's call to submit to governing authorities, Romans 13:1, as well as the counsel to pray for those in authority, 1 Timothy 2:1 to 2, takes up Jeremiah's pattern. The warning against false teachers who offer comfort without truth runs from 2 Peter 2:1 to 1 John 4:1, and the test of the prophet's word has its New Testament parallel in 1 John 4:1: 'test the spirits to see whether they are from God.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted the exiles and the people still in Jerusalem to see that the difference between a true and a false prophet is not tone, popularity, confidence or office but whether the message agrees with God's earlier word and with what He is actually doing. Hananiah has every outward credential. He is a recognised prophet, he speaks in the temple, he uses the formula, and he offers hope the people badly want. What he lacks is God's commission, 'The LORD did not send you,' 28:15. The chapter teaches that a message of peace, the very thing that people most want to hear, needs more proof than a message of judgment, because it has to overcome the weight of the prophetic tradition, 28:8.

It also teaches how a true prophet acts under pressure. Jeremiah does not match Hananiah's volume. He wishes him well, 'Amen! May the LORD do so,' 28:6, and he yields the stage when his yoke is broken, 28:11. Only when God speaks does he answer. The first hearers were meant to learn patience in a hard word: the yoke will be borne, the exile will last, and survival lies in serving, 27:12.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The text describes a political situation, a prophetic sign act and a dispute. It does not teach that every nation should submit to every empire, or that believers should never resist unjust rule. The command to serve Babylon is a specific word to a specific people in a specific year, for a stated period, 27:7. The same book shows Jeremiah later telling the people to surrender in order to live, Jeremiah 38:2, because God had given them into Babylon's hand, not because Babylon was good.

The lasting application is about discernment. The test Jeremiah gives, 'only if the word of the prophet comes true,' 28:9, applies to prophets who promise peace, and the New Testament asks the church to weigh what is said, 1 Thessalonians 5:20 to 21, and to hold to the apostles' teaching rather than to charm. And the modest application on submission is to pair it with Acts 5:29, 'We must obey God rather than men,' so that the believer's obedience to rulers is real but bounded. Nothing here licences a prophet to curse a rival, or a church to treat popularity as proof.

debates.question: What is the test of a true prophet, and does Jeremiah 28:9 settle it?

views.label: Fulfilment is the decisive test
views.case: Deuteronomy 18:22 says that a message that does not come true is not from the LORD, and Jeremiah 28:9 applies it. Hananiah's two-year prediction was disproved by the events of 586, and his own death within the year was the immediate sign. This view takes the passage at face value as a rule for the test.

views.label: Fulfilment is necessary but not sufficient
views.case: Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5 shows that a sign can come true and the prophet still be false if he leads people from the LORD. Jeremiah himself says peace-prophets have not been sent, 23:21 and 28:15, and judges them by their content, 23:22. So the full test is both whether the prophet's word agrees with the God of the covenant and whether it comes to pass.

views.label: Fulfilment is a test only for a particular kind of prophecy
views.case: Because Jeremiah says that the prophets of old announced war and disaster, 28:8, and that only the peace-prophet needs to be verified, some note that threats can be withdrawn on repentance, as in Jeremiah 18:7 to 10, so that an unfulfilled threat does not prove a prophet false. Jonah is the standard example. The test in 28:9 is thus specific to promises.

debates.bearing: The three views together warn against simple rules. A message must be tested by Scripture, by its fruit and by time, and no single check is enough.

debates.question: Is Jeremiah's call to submit to Babylon a general teaching about obedience to government?

views.label: A particular command for a particular moment
views.case: God's appointment of Nebuchadnezzar, 27:6, and its limit, 'until the time of his own land comes,' 27:7, make this a historic word. Nothing in it tells later believers to submit to every power. Jeremiah's own later counsel to surrender is rooted in the same specific word, Jeremiah 38:2.

views.label: An instance of a wider biblical pattern
views.case: God sets up and removes rulers, Daniel 2:21, and the New Testament counsels submission, Romans 13:1 and 1 Peter 2:13. On this view Jeremiah gives the Old Testament root of Paul's teaching, with its same warning: authority is God's, and so is its judgment.

views.label: A limited submission with a clear boundary
views.case: Revelation 13 pictures a state that demands worship and invites patient endurance, 13:10, and Acts 5:29 gives the limit. Daniel's refusal to worship the image, Daniel 3, shows that service to Babylon never included a command to disobey God.

debates.bearing: The passage joins the first and third views: serve where service does not betray God, and trust Him for the length of the yoke.

study.originalLanguages:
The yoke itself is made of two parts in 27:2, straps and bars, and 28:10 and 28:13 speak of the bars of the yoke. The same word for bars appears in Leviticus 26:13, 'I broke the bars of your yoke,' where it is a promise of freedom. In 28:13 Hananiah breaks bars of wood, and God answers that he has made bars of iron. The word choice shows that the prophet's act, taken from the exodus language of liberation, is being turned against the one who borrowed it.

The warning of 27:8 uses the triple of sword, famine and plague, in Hebrew chereb, ra'av and dever, a formula that Jeremiah uses again and again, 14:12 and 21:7 among others. The surprising point is that it comes with a way out: the nation that serves lives, 27:11, an echo of Deuteronomy's choice of life and death, Deuteronomy 30:19.

In 28:8 and 28:9 the contrast is between prophets of 'war, disaster and plague' and the one who prophesies 'peace,' shalom. The word is the greatest word of blessing in Israel, and Hananiah's misuse of it is what makes his lie so dangerous. Jeremiah 6:14 and 8:11 have already named the offence: healing the wound lightly, saying 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.

The phrase 'within two years' in 28:3 and 28:11 is literally 'two years of days,' the idiom for a full two years, as in Genesis 41:1. Hananiah gives a round and checkable timetable, and Jeremiah's reply has the same verifiable form, 'You will die this year,' 28:16.

The verb in 28:15 for 'trust' is the causal form, 'you have made this people trust,' and the accusation is therefore that Hananiah acted on their faith. What the people trusted is, in Hebrew, 'a lie,' sheqer, and the verb 'persuaded' is exactly what made it dangerous. The final charge in 28:16, 'you have preached rebellion,' uses the word sarah, the same word as in Deuteronomy 13:5, where a false prophet is condemned for advocating rebellion against the LORD. The chapter thus applies the Torah's capital charge to Hananiah and records the sentence in 28:17.

One textual note is worth knowing. The Septuagint translation of Jeremiah is shorter than the Hebrew text and numbers these chapters 34 and 35, so readers who use a Greek Old Testament will find the passage under different numbers.

typology.type: The yoke of wood and the yoke of iron
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah's wooden yoke is a sign of an imposed burden that God has appointed, and Hananiah's breaking of it only produces a heavier one. Jesus, in Matthew 11:29 to 30, invites the weary to take His yoke, which is easy, and Peter calls the law a yoke that neither fathers nor children could bear, Acts 15:10. Paul says that Christ has set believers free so that they should not be burdened again by a yoke of slavery, Galatians 5:1. The escalation is that Christ's yoke is a relationship, not a sentence. The type falls short because Babylon's yoke was deserved punishment, while Christ's is given in grace.

typology.type: Hananiah, the prophet of false peace
typology.fulfillment: Hananiah's confident comfort in the temple, 'I have broken the yoke,' pictures the false teachers whom the New Testament warns about. Peter says they will bring in destructive heresies and exploit people with false words, 2 Peter 2:1 to 3, and Paul describes those who will not endure sound teaching but gather teachers to suit their own desires, 2 Timothy 4:3. The escalation is that the true Prophet announces peace through blood, Colossians 1:20, not peace without repentance. The type falls short in that Hananiah's end came within the year, while the final judgment of false teachers is still ahead.

typology.type: The temple vessels carried to Babylon and promised back
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah says that the remaining vessels will go to Babylon and stay 'until the day I attend to them again,' 27:22, and Ezra 1:7 to 11 records Cyrus returning them. The vessels are a type of what God keeps and restores in His time. In Christ the true temple is raised, John 2:19 to 21, and the people themselves become God's dwelling, 1 Corinthians 3:16. The type falls short because the vessels were returned to a building that would again be destroyed, while the new temple cannot be.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ most directly in the matter of the yoke. Jesus says, 'Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls,' Matthew 11:29. The word 'learn' is the language of a disciple, and the 'rest' recalls the people of Jeremiah 6:16 who were told to find rest for their souls and refused. The wooden yoke Jeremiah wore was a sentence to be borne in obedience, and Jesus offers Himself as the one under whose authority the burden turns light. The contrast with Hananiah is exact. Hananiah promised release without repentance and delivered a heavier bondage. Jesus asks for submission and delivers freedom, John 8:36.

It leads to Christ by the test of the true prophet. Hananiah's oracle failed, and Jeremiah's word stood. Jesus is the Prophet in whom the test is passed perfectly, Deuteronomy 18:18 to 19 and Acts 3:22, since every word He spoke came true, from the prediction of the temple's fall, Luke 21:6, to the promise of His own resurrection, Matthew 16:21 and 28:6. Peter's proof that He was no false teacher is that God raised Him.

It leads to Christ by the figure of the servant under a foreign yoke. In Jeremiah, Nebuchadnezzar is called God's servant, 27:6, but in the book of Isaiah the true Servant of the LORD takes the yoke of others' sin upon Himself, Isaiah 53:4 to 6. He did not break the bonds of God's people with a hammer, but bore the penalty that bound them, 1 Peter 2:24.

It leads to Christ by the truth about peace. Hananiah gave a cheap peace, and Jeremiah's earlier word had called that peace a deception, Jeremiah 6:14. Jesus says, 'My peace I give you; I do not give to you as the world gives,' John 14:27, and Paul says that we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, Romans 5:1, and that He Himself is our peace, Ephesians 2:14. That peace is real because the debt was paid, not ignored.

A caution is needed. The chapter is not a coded picture of Jesus. Jeremiah's yoke is not the cross, and Nebuchadnezzar is not a type of Christ. The links hold because the New Testament itself takes up the image of the yoke, the test of the prophet and the true peace, and sets the answers in Jesus.
study.god:
The chapter's boldest claim about God is in 27:5 to 6: the Creator who made the earth 'by My great power and outstretched arm' gives it 'to whom I please,' and has put the lands under Nebuchadnezzar's authority. This is the sovereignty of the Maker over the map. It is not an endorsement of Babylon, who will be judged in turn, 27:7, but a refusal to let Judah think that history is out of His hands. It also takes the sting from the shock: the catastrophe that frightens them is not the failure of God but the working of God.

He is a God of truth who defends His own word against forgery. 'I have not sent them,' 27:15, and 'The LORD did not send you,' 28:15, show that the prophetic office is not a human possession. The same God allows the false prophet to speak, to break the yoke before the crowd and to look victorious for a moment. Then He answers, and the answer comes by His own timing, within the year. Jeremiah's patience in verse 11, going his way until the word came, is the patience of someone who knows that God defends His truth.

He is also a God who offers life even under judgment. 'Serve him and live,' 27:12, is as much a gracious offer as a command. The nation that bows will stay in its own land, 27:11, and the remaining vessels, now in the temple, will be returned in the end, 27:22. Even the threat of Babylon is bounded: 'until the time of his own land comes,' 27:7. God holds judgment and restoration in one hand.

He is just. The sentence on Hananiah, who has persuaded the people to trust a lie, 28:15, shows that teaching falsehood in God's name is a grave offence, because the cost is the people's lives. And He is kind to the true prophet, whose silence He breaks with a word.

For worship, the passage teaches us to trust the God who rules the nations rather than to hope in the strength of rulers, and to pray for the courage to say unwelcome things. It teaches us to wait for Him to vindicate His own word instead of rushing to do it for Him.

crossReferences.note: The root of the yoke language. God says He broke the bars of Israel's yoke when He brought them out of Egypt. Hananiah's 'I have broken the yoke' borrows the exodus language of liberation, and Jeremiah's iron yoke is its covenant reversal.

The curse of an iron yoke for covenant breaking. Jeremiah 28:13 is the fulfilment of this warning, which shows that Hananiah's comfortable word ignores the terms of the covenant his own people had accepted.

The law of the prophet who speaks presumptuously, and the test of fulfilment. Jeremiah 28:9 applies it, and 28:16 applies the penalty. It shows the passage is reasoned from Torah and not simply a clash of personalities.

The prophet or dreamer who leads people astray, even with a sign that comes true. The word 'rebellion' in Jeremiah 28:16 is the charge made here, and the passage is a reminder that a true sign alone does not prove a true message.

Later in Zedekiah's reign Jeremiah repeats the same counsel in the siege: whoever surrenders will live. It shows the yoke message was no passing mood but the consistent word of the prophet until the city fell.

God calls Cyrus His anointed, as He calls Nebuchadnezzar His servant in Jeremiah 27:6. Both show that foreign rulers can be instruments in God's hand without sharing His covenant, and that He moves them as He wills.

Cyrus brings out the temple vessels and has them counted for Sheshbazzar. It fulfils the promise of Jeremiah 27:22 that God would bring the vessels back, and it shows the true prophet's word standing after the false prophet's was disproved.

Jesus invites the weary to His yoke. Set beside Jeremiah's, it shows the difference between a yoke imposed as discipline and a yoke offered as a gift, and it makes Jesus the answer to the longing that Hananiah exploited.

Paul's teaching on submission to governing authorities as appointed by God. It reads like a New Testament application of Jeremiah 27:5 to 6, in which God gives rule to whom He pleases, though the passage in Jeremiah is more specific and time-limited.

Warns of false teachers who will exploit people with fabricated words. Hananiah is an Old Testament instance of just this, and Peter's reminder that their judgment is not idle matches the swift sentence in Jeremiah 28:16 to 17.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with a creator who gave humanity dominion over the earth, Genesis 1:28, and with a first temptation that came as a question about what God had said, Genesis 3:1. Every false prophet since works in the same way: a plausible voice that makes the word of God doubtful or negotiable. Hananiah is that voice in Zion, and his message is the oldest one, that God will let us off.

In the middle of the story the pattern becomes national. The exodus broke Israel's yoke, Leviticus 26:13, and the covenant warned that disobedience would bring an iron one, Deuteronomy 28:48. Jeremiah 27 and 28 are where that warning is fulfilled in history. The nation that had been freed from Pharaoh serves Nebuchadnezzar, and the prophet who sees it is the one the people do not want to hear. Yet the same chapters carry a hidden promise: the servitude has a limit, 27:7, the vessels will return, 27:22, and the next chapters turn to the letter to the exiles and the Book of Consolation, where God promises to break the yoke Himself, Jeremiah 30:8.

The story reaches its centre in the One who took the yoke on Himself. Jesus came to a people under Rome's rule who longed for a hammer to break the yoke, and offered a different liberation, one that began with a heart and a cross, Luke 4:18 and Mark 10:45. He did not promise that the empire would fall in two years. He promised that the kingdom had come and would come.

The new creation ends the contest of yokes. Revelation records the fall of the great Babylon, Revelation 18:2, and the end of the nations' servitude to powers that deceive, Revelation 20:3. The people of God, who once wore the yoke of exile, will reign with Christ, Revelation 22:5, and the false prophets will have no place, Revelation 21:8 and 22:15. The peace that Hananiah could only claim will be a real thing: 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah's wooden yoke symbolize in this passage?

options.text: Submission to Babylon's rule as God's appointed discipline for Judah and the surrounding nations.
options.note: God explicitly calls Nebuchadnezzar 'My servant' and commands submission to his rule for a set time.

options.text: A call to immediate armed rebellion against Babylon.
options.note: The message is the opposite, submit to Babylon's yoke rather than resist it.

options.text: A purely private symbol with no message for other nations.
options.note: The message is explicitly sent to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon as well as Judah.

options.text: A sign that Judah's temple would never be destroyed.
options.note: The yoke concerns political submission to Babylon, not a promise about the temple's permanence.

quiz.q: What does Hananiah publicly do and prophesy in chapter 28?

options.text: He breaks Jeremiah's yoke and prophesies that within two years Babylon's rule and the exile will be over.
options.note: Verses 2 to 4 and 10 to 11 record both the symbolic act and the specific two-year timeframe.

options.text: He affirms Jeremiah's message and adds further warnings of judgment.
options.note: Hananiah directly contradicts Jeremiah's message, promising the opposite, quick deliverance.

options.text: He requests to see Jeremiah's yoke without commenting on its meaning.
options.note: He actively breaks the yoke and delivers a specific counter-prophecy.

options.text: He predicts a hundred years of continued Babylonian rule.
options.note: His specific prediction is a two-year timeframe for the yoke's end, not a hundred years.

quiz.q: What test does Jeremiah give for discerning a true prophet in verse 9?

options.text: A prophet who prophesies peace is recognized as truly sent by the LORD only if the word comes true.
options.note: This echoes the test given in Deuteronomy 18:21-22, fulfillment proves the source of the word.

options.text: A true prophet is recognized by how confidently he speaks.
options.note: Confidence of delivery is explicitly not the test; fulfillment is the standard given.

options.text: A true prophet is recognized by popular approval alone.
options.note: Hananiah appears to have had popular support, yet his message is proven false.

options.text: A true prophet must always prophesy disaster, never peace.
options.note: The text distinguishes prophets of old who spoke disaster from this specific test about peace-prophecies, not a blanket rule against ever prophesying peace.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate outcome of Hananiah breaking the wooden yoke?

options.text: God declares an iron yoke will replace the wooden one, and Hananiah himself dies within the year for preaching a lie.
options.note: Verses 13 to 17 record both the harsher judgment and Hananiah's specific death that same year.

options.text: The yoke of Babylon is permanently removed exactly as Hananiah predicted.
options.note: The opposite occurs; God announces an even harsher yoke of iron.

options.text: Jeremiah is punished instead of Hananiah for the broken yoke.
options.note: The judgment falls specifically and explicitly on Hananiah, not Jeremiah.

options.text: Nothing further happens; the incident is never resolved in the text.
options.note: Verse 17 explicitly records Hananiah's death that same year, resolving the confrontation.

quiz.q: How does Christ's teaching about His own yoke connect to this passage?

options.text: Christ offers His own yoke as easy and light, the ultimate contrast to Babylon's heavy yoke and Hananiah's false promise of easy liberation.
options.note: Matthew 11:29-30 deliberately uses the same yoke image in direct contrast to every burdensome or false yoke.

options.text: There is no connection between Christ's teaching and the yoke imagery in Jeremiah.
options.note: Matthew 11:29-30 uses the identical image of a yoke, inviting direct comparison.

options.text: Christ's yoke is described as even heavier than Babylon's.
options.note: Christ explicitly describes His yoke as easy and His burden as light, the opposite of heavier.

options.text: The connection is only that both involve farming equipment.
options.note: The connection is theological, submission and rest, not merely a shared agricultural tool.

questions: Hananiah's message was popular and comforting, but it was not from God. Where might you be drawn to a comforting message over a true one right now?

God called submission to Babylon's yoke, though painful, the path to life rather than destruction. Is there a hard circumstance you are resisting that God may actually be calling you to accept as His discipline?
Jeremiah's test for a true prophet was whether the word actually came true. How do you test the messages and promises you hear against God's revealed word rather than simply their appeal?
Hananiah's false liberation led only to a heavier yoke. Where have you seen a shortcut or comfortable lie ultimately cost more than the harder truth would have?
Christ offers His people a yoke that is genuinely easy and light. Where do you need to exchange a burden you are carrying on your own for genuine submission to Him?

translationNotes.note: 'Him and his son and grandson' reflects the actual succession of Babylonian kings after Nebuchadnezzar, showing this prophecy anticipated a limited, multi-generational span of Babylonian dominance rather than permanent rule.

Jeremiah's 'Amen! May the LORD do so!' expresses genuine longing for restoration to be true, not agreement with Hananiah's claim that it was already accomplished; the very next verses immediately qualify this with a substantive test of the prophecy's truth.

Hananiah's death 'in the seventh month of that very year' came just two months after his confrontation with Jeremiah in the fifth month, verse 1, a rapid and public vindication of Jeremiah's word within the same year.
